## Episode 1303 — How Can I Doubt My Doubts? (Part II)
Published: 2023-10-16
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/doubts-part-ii/

Matthew 28:16-17: (KJV) 16 Then the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, into a mountain where Jesus had appointed them. 17 And when they saw him, they worshipped him: but some doubted.

In our previous episode, we discussed doubt as a permanent fixture in our present world and experiences and how this can be both positive as well as negative. There are many ways the seeds of doubt are planted. We can doubt as a result of misinformation or misunderstanding. We can doubt when we have a limited perception of our circumstances. We can doubt when we are in a difficult situation or have unmet expectations. Whatever the case may be, doubt is a very real part of our Christian experience. As we continue our conversation in this episode, we will focus on how doubt manifested itself in the New Testament and what we can learn from it. To clearly understand doubt is to open the door that can diffuse it or use it, whichever brings glory to God!

There is good doubt and bad doubt. On our last episode, we talked about the DESTRUCTIVE DOUBT of Eve and Israel. Both doubted God. - Eve’s doubt was brought on by the authority of Lucifer (Satan).

This was misinformation. - Israel’s doubt was brought on by serious physical need.

This was a difficult situation.

We also talked about the CONSTRUCTIVE DOUBT of Gideon and John the Baptist. Yes, doubt can be beneficial! - Gideon’s doubt was brought on by being given a task that he perceived to be far beyond his capacity. Gideon had limited perception. - John the Baptist’s doubt was stimulated by his unrealized expectation of how Jesus’ teachings would change the world. John had unmet expectations.

These four examples of doubt give us a broad base on which to build. As we now discuss doubt in the New Testament, we want to draw a specific line of understanding. We will be examining doubts that have the potential to be diffused or bring us to growth and we will spend very little time discussing blatant disbelief.

When Jesus was on the cross, the Pharisees were strong examples of this kind of blatant disbelief:

Matthew 27:41-43: 41 In the same way the chief priests also, along with the scribes and elders, were mocking him and saying, 42 He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the king of Israel; let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe in him (They quote from the Old Testament - Psalm 22: 8). 43 He trusts in God; let God rescue him now, if He delights in him; for he said I am the son of God.

These religious rulers knew the prophecies of the Messiah and used this one to taunt him, which is ironic because in doing so, they said exactly what was prophesied they would say. Psalm 22 prophetically describes Jesus’ experience on the cross.

Psalms 22:6-8: 6 But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people. 7 All who see me sneer at me; they separate with the lip, they wag the head, saying, 8 Commit yourself to the Lord; let Him deliver him; let Him rescue him, because He delights in him.

The Pharisees’ “offer” to believe in Jesus if he came down from the cross was only a gesture of mockery. What cruelty and loss of human compassion! Jesus was too much of a threat to the Pharisees. They were trying to protect their religious standing with the people. Their hatred was doubt gone bad. They took anything Jesus did or said out of context. Their hearts were so hardened that their doubts would never turn to trust and then to faith. We can certainly encounter people like this in our own witnessing efforts. There is nothing we can do or say that will get them to follow Jesus in this lifetime, and that’s okay. When their eyes are opened in God’s kingdom, they will have an opportunity to learn and repent.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: The Pharisees did not doubt Jesus; they despised him. They grudgingly witnessed his miracles, were stymied by his teachings and were struck speechless by his questions. What may have begun as doubt on some level degraded into a seething anger that would only be satisfied with the utter destruction and humiliation of Jesus and his teachings. Let us NEVER allow ourselves to fall so low as this treatment of another, because God, not us, is the Judge of all.

There are several New Testament words that show us doubt on different levels. We will start with what looks like the mildest kinds of doubt. This first word, diakrino, has many shades of meaning: Doubt: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1252 diakrino; to separate thoroughly, i.e. (literally and reflexively) to withdraw from, or (by implication) oppose; figuratively, to discriminate (by implication, decide), or (reflexively) hesitate King James Version translates this word as doubt 5 times, judge 3 times, discern 2 times, contend 2 times, waver 2 times, in a miscellaneous way 5 times Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to separate, make a distinction, discriminate, to prefer

2) to learn by discrimination, to try, decide 2a) to determine, give judgment, decide a dispute 3) to withdraw from one, desert 4) to separate one’s self in a hostile spirit, to oppose, strive with dispute, contend 5) to be at variance with one’s self, hesitate, doubt We found something interesting overall about the Greek words used for doubt. Diakrino - The first two letters in English are “di.” In Greek, this “di” prefix indicates “two,” “twice,” “double.”

Our English word “dilemma” comes from ancient Greek, having two of, specifically, an ambiguous proposition. A dilemma is a difficult situation requiring a choice. The way diakrino is used scripturally is positive, in that at least there is a choice, as opposed to having no way out.

This is a general word used in a variety of ways.

This is a general word used in a variety of ways. For example:

1 Corinthians 6:4-6: 4 So if you have law courts dealing with matters of this life, do you appoint them as judges who are of no account in the church? 5 I say this to your shame. Is it so, that there is not among you one wise man who will be able to decide <1252> between his brethren, 6 but brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers?

The word translated as decide is the same word for doubt. There is a duality to deciding; it can go in either direction.

This kind of doubt has different options. There is not among you one wise man who will be able to decide between his brethren - As Christians, we should be able to find someone in the church who is able to decide between our brethren who have a dispute, someone who can separate out the truth of the matter. We should not need to go to the law when we have each other. We are supposed to be living by higher standards.

Now on to the meanings that reflect doubt:

James 1:5-8: 5 But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him. 6 But he must ask in faith without any doubting <1252>, for the one who doubts is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. 7 For that man ought not to expect that he will receive anything from the Lord, 8 being a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

Using the surf of the sea tossing us around is a great analogy. Double-minded means going back and forth between two opinions or influences. We might lean one way but do not really take a stand. Many people end up taking the path of least resistance because it is easier than fighting against our own natural tendencies.

James brings up that a double-minded man, one who is driven and tossed by various opinions, is unstable in all his ways. This is a “no trespass” territory for Christians. We are never to ever be double-minded.

It is one thing to have faith. It is another thing to apply that faith in a firm, unhesitating and single-minded way. Our natural tendencies are not necessarily going to align with what we know to be spiritual Christian faith. We have to choose instead of wavering and hesitating - Do I like it this way…? No! I need to decide to go that way instead!

A prime example of single-minded faith is Abraham. Here’s what his unhesitating faith looked like:

Romans 4:19-22: 19 Without becoming weak in faith he contemplated his own body, now as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb; 20 yet, with respect to the promise of God, he did not waver <1252> in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, 21 and being fully assured that what God had promised, He was able also to perform. 22 Therefore it was also credited to him as righteousness.

The fact was they were clearly too old to have a baby. But Abraham believed the promise of God over the fact of their age. He didn’t need more information. While he knew it was physically impossible, he also knew God would find a way.

What stands in the way becomes the way. — Roman Emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius.

Our doubts can become obstacles or tools.

It is interesting the way Abraham's challenge and victory is presented here. He did not waiver in unbelief, the kind of unbelief the Pharisees had. Abraham did not vacillate between thinking either it can never happen or maybe it will happen. He went with God's word. That is the understanding we need to grab hold of when there is this hesitation. What is God's unequivocal word?

This is why it was credited to him as righteousness. When we look at our lives and our many reasons for hesitating, do they begin to stack up against the impossibility of Abraham's circumstances? When we are vacillating back and forth, think about Abraham and the massive steps of faith he continually took, and how blessed he was as a result.

It is imperative to make sure we identify any of our double-mindedness and find the higher, godly road to follow. This is how doubt gets put in its proper place. We have been called to serve God through following Jesus. Heeding this call means we need to be very aware of what we pay attention to.

Being single-minded in serving God is our main objective.

Are there times this single-mindedness can bring us trouble?

The beauty of growing and maturing as a Christian is that there is always something else to learn. We can live a life dedicated to God’s will, and in our experiences we will regularly be tested so that dedication can continually grow stronger. Our doubts in this process can be true steppingstones to a more Christlike character.

Let’s look at doubt in a more positive light by examining another New Testament word that’s on the milder side.

Doubt: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1365 distazo; from #1364 (which means twice); properly, to duplicate, i.e. (mentally) to waver (in opinion) King James Version translates this word: doubt 2 times Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to doubt, waver This Greek word also starts with a “di” prefix and comes from a different word that means “twice.” I can go this way or that way, so which is the more godly direction? This word is only used twice in the New Testament, and both uses provide significant lessons.

The first use is the Apostle Peter walking towards Jesus on water. Let’s read the verse where the doubt is revealed and then go back and build the story behind it:

Matthew 14:30-31: 30 But seeing the wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, Lord, save me! 31 Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him, and said to him, you of little faith, why did you doubt <1365>?

In other words: Why did you waver? Why did you hesitate? Some think Jesus said this as a rebuke or out of pity. But that’s not what it sounds like when you read the context and understand what this word for doubt means.

Why did you doubt?

Jesus is making a positive statement, as we can see from the full account:

Matthew 14:22-33: 22 Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away. 23 After he had sent the crowds away, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray; and when it was evening, he was there alone.

This was after the miraculous “feeding of the 5,000,” which incidentally, is the only miracle aside from Jesus’ own resurrection that is recorded in all four gospels.

Jesus multiplied five barley loaves and two fish into enough food to feed 5,000 men and an unknown number of women and children – and there were even leftovers!

After demonstrating such power, no wonder Jesus needed a moment to himself to pray to his Father and rejuvenate. It would also give his disciples time to talk it over by themselves and think about the miracle that just occurred.

Jesus had just demonstrated the impossible and shown everyone that God’s spirit in him could accomplish things beyond their imaginations: 24 But the boat was already a long distance from the land, battered by the waves; for the wind was contrary. 25 And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. 26 When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, it is a spirit! And they cried out in fear.

The fourth watch of the night is between 3am and 6am. They have been rowing for hours against the wind and the waves, they are worn out and hanging on, and now in their exhaustion see some scary figure walking towards them on the water. Even though they were experienced fishermen, rough seas in the middle of the night were a dramatic concern.

Seeing a figure upon these tumultuous waters turned concern to a bewildered fear: 27 But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid. We can imagine they are trying to figure out how Jesus is talking to them when he’s not in the boat! None of it makes any sense! 28 Peter said to him, Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. 29 And he said, Come!

In the face of fear and uncertainty, Peter is willing to suspend his trust in the natural laws of the earth and place all of his trust upon his Lord Jesus.

It sounds like instead of having little faith, Peter had BIG faith! He trusted it was Jesus - so much so that he actually got out of the boat and stepped into the water in the middle of a dangerous windstorm! Think about that for a moment! Who does that? ...And Peter got out of the boat, and walked on the water and came toward Jesus. 30 But seeing the wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, Lord, save me! Peter is doing the impossible! It is physically beyond the realm of reality to do what Peter is doing. And yet, by a miracle, by God’s spirit, he IS doing it. But as he is walking toward Jesus, he sees the wind.

It would be hard to not “see the wind” because it is smacking him in the face! When he was in the boat he had something to hang on to, but out there in the elements there was nothing near him except Jesus who, several steps away, seemed out of reach in that moment.

Fear brought doubt, and doubt swung his focus to the overwhelming elements that surrounded him – doubt took his focus away from his objective. Doubt will do that to us, and Peter is a dramatic example. 31 Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him, and said to him, You of little faith, why did you doubt <1365>? 32 When they got into the boat, the wind stopped. 33 And those who were in the boat worshiped him, saying, you are certainly God's son! Not only did Jesus rescue Peter, but the wind stopped altogether! There is an immediate paradigm shift in the circumstances. This is Jesus showing the power of God’s spirit within him. This is Jesus showing what he had been continually showing them throughout his ministry with the miracles, the feeding of the 5,000 and with all the other things they saw him do. This was just another way to see the ability of Jesus wielding God’s spirit within him.

Why would Jesus say Peter had little faith when Peter did what no one else dared to do?

- Perhaps it was because Peter’s faith was strong enough to begin but was not trusting enough to finish.
- Perhaps it was because Peter momentarily lost his focus on where he was called to go. It says but seeing the wind, he became frightened. Once that happened, he began to sink! It was downhill from there.
- Perhaps it was because this was not the first time the apostles witnessed Jesus’ power through God’s spirit over those very same elements. A previous miracle on the water is when the disciples and Jesus were in the boat, there was a storm, the boat was covered with waves and Jesus was sleeping:

Matthew 8:25-27: 25 And they came to him and woke him, saying, save us, Lord; we are perishing! 26 He said to them, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith? Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and it became perfectly calm. 27 The men were amazed, and said, what kind of a man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?

Notice that in this account, nobody responds to the question Jesus asked, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith? They are in awe. Their faith has actually been stimulated to grow because they saw something so out of control, and yet Jesus, through God’s spirit, was able to bring it back under control.

Jesus uses the phrase ye men of little faith four different times. It is never said in an insulting way, as in Oh, grow up! Instead, he says it in the sense of, You have something valuable; let me show you how to grow it into something much larger.

This is how we can understand that Peter’s doubt helped him grow.

The Sea of Galilee is actually a lake about 700 feet below sea level. It’s about 12 miles long and seven miles wide surrounded by a high and almost unbroken wall of hills. These hills are pierced by deep canyons and ravines, which under certain atmospheric conditions, act like gigantic funnels to draw down the cold winds from the mountains that expose the sea to frequent and sudden violent storms, even to this day.

There is one more incredible aspect of this miracle: It’s not so much that Jesus stopped the wind – wind can stop suddenly under natural conditions. The most astonishing part is the lake water suddenly being as calm as glass. After a violent storm, all of the energy in the waves don’t just stop. The waves crash for hours or even days afterwards as the energy slowly dissipates.

Even the wind and the sea obey him — in this we see a powerful display of what God’s spirit and influence can do. Peter doubted, and Jesus’ response was, you of little faith, why did you doubt? Rather than being negative, this was a growing experience for Peter and the others in the boat.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: The Apostle Peter’s doubt as he walked on the water should be an inspiration to us. His faith brought him to engage in the impossible. Jesus’ rescue of Peter and his reminder to Peter of the power of strong faith in the midst of chaos brought Peter to see how much more he could grow.

If we were in Peter’s place and Jesus had to rescue us, would we be thinking, Why did I doubt? I should know better. Jesus is right in front of me. I am not going to forget next time! I am not going to look away next time. I will only look at Jesus. This is how CONSTRUCTIVE DOUBT works in us. Jesus is also using this doubt to stimulate growth in us.

After Jesus’ resurrection, this same kind of doubt or wavering was present:

Matthew 28:16-18: 16 But the eleven disciples proceeded to Galilee, to the mountain which Jesus had designated. 17 When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some were doubtful <1365>. 18 And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, all authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.

Many times Jesus told the disciples he was leaving and going to his Father in heaven. Maybe this doubt some were having was because they knew he was leaving them that day. Maybe they were thinking, Something is happening here that we don’t understand; this will be different and not what we expected. We don't know what to do when he’s gone. The last verse in Matthew says, Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. That gives the answer to that doubt. But, of course, they were not able to grasp this.

After all Jesus had taught, after all he had done, after all he had been through, doubt still had a hold upon some. Again, why? We all face the continual challenge of reframing our fleshly minds toward spiritual things. We are all stuck in that vortex of the fleshly mind pulling us back while we attempt to walk towards spiritual things.

This does not have to be a catastrophic doubt. This kind of CONSTRUCTIVE DOUBT should be a learning experience. The apostles learned quickly how it would be when Jesus was not with them physically.

Let’s take a look at doubt in a bigger way.

Everyone has their own doubts, whether expressed or secret. Again, our doubts might come as a result of misinformation or misunderstanding or from a limited perception of our circumstances. We might be in an unusually difficult situation, or have unmet expectations.

It is important to realize that all of these reactions are natural outcomes of our human nature. By understanding this is natural and not something to destroy us, we can use doubt to plant a good seed in fertile ground so it can grow. This is what Peter did after walking on the water and what the apostles did when they were doubtful of where Jesus would be after his crucifixion.

We might just have the type of personality that is naturally more skeptical than others. Past betrayals or periods of high stress can lead to more doubt and make us less apt to trust people or have confidence in what we thought we knew.

For our listeners and readers going through a time of exceptionally high doubt, we suggest going back to the five questions we presented in Part I to consider: - WHAT OR WHOM AM I DOUBTING? - IS THIS DOUBT PRIMARILY BASED ON MY HEART BEING TROUBLED? - IS THIS DOUBT PRIMARILY BASED ON MY MIND NOT SEEING OR UNDERSTANDING? - WHAT BRINGS THIS DOUBT TO MY HEART OR MIND? - DOES THIS DOUBT HELP MY CHRISTIAN EXPERIENCE OR HINDER MY CHRISTIAN EXPERIENCE?

Using these questions comes down to being honest enough to look at the “why” of our doubt. If we take our doubt apart with scriptural principles in hand, it will be so much easier to put it back together. Then maybe we can be privileged to be the O you of little faith who can grow into something so much bigger than we were before.

This is the big question. When we have doubts, where does our mind go? Does it go to Jesus, whom we are called to follow, doing what we are called to do? Or does it dwell in wallowing in the doubt and the I don’t know. Maybe we don’t know, but who does? Our Father in heaven knows, and His providence provides.

It’s hard to imagine more dramatic circumstances where faith can be tested than walking on the water or seeing the risen Lord!

So far, we have seen doubt defined as hesitation and wavering.

How much deeper can our doubt as Christians go?

The next level of doubt presents a broader challenge. As we shall see, it is bigger than hesitation and wavering. We shall also see that when this next level of doubt is present in Jesus’ disciples or potential disciples, it is always given a very clear explanation. We want to pay close attention to the kinds of lessons this combination will teach us. This next level of doubt we will look at is from a Greek word diaporeo: Loss: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1280 diaporeo; to be thoroughly nonplussed King James Version translates this word as doubt 2 times, be perplexed 1 time, be much perplexed 1 time, be in doubt 1 time Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to be entirely at loss, to be in perplexity The Greek word diaporeo has another “di” prefix, so we know there is still a sense of having choices. In the next examples of how this word is used, we note that when this sudden shock kind of doubt or puzzlement happens, a dramatic explanation follows to help the shocked person move forward.

Nonplussed means: To be so surprised or confused that you are not sure how to react. Perplexed.

The first time this perplexed kind of doubt appears in relation to Christianity is right after Jesus’ resurrection:

Luke 24:1-7: 1 But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they came to the tomb bringing the spices which they had prepared. 2 And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, 3 but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. 4 While they were perplexed <1280> about this...

This group of women, who included Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary, the mother of James, (Luke 24:10) are here to bring spices to the tomb like we would bring flowers today, and the body is gone! They were in the right place, because they had followed Jesus’ body being placed there in the previous chapter (Luke 23:55). What happened? HOW could this happen? What did they do with him? ...behold, two men suddenly stood near them in dazzling clothing; 5 and as the women were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, Why do you seek the living one among the dead? 6 He is not here, but he has risen. Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, 7 saying that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again.

We learn from the accounts in Matthew and John that these men…in dazzling clothing were angels. The women were immediately given an explanation for their sudden shock - He is risen.

This was a big moment in Christian history, and with a big answer. There was serious perplexity in the context of unmet expectations. The women were on their way to honor the dead body of Jesus. He wasn’t there, and they had no idea what to do with the circumstance. Immediately they receive a spiritual answer.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: Sometimes we are clear in what to expect, and yet perplexing doubt arises that contradicts our expectations. Let us be open to the guidance of God’s word through whatever means it is clarified to us as we learn to pause, consider and refocus.

What did these women do immediately after this experience? They refocused. Now, instead of bringing spices to the tomb to anoint their Lord’s dead body, they ran back to the apostles and told them of his resurrection.

We see that incredible refocus – their perplexity brought them to the most wonderful expectation they could possibly have that was beyond what they could have seen.

Let’s look at what happened immediately at Pentecost after the disciples spoke in tongues:

Acts 2:12-16: 12 And they all continued in amazement and great perplexity <1280>, saying to one another, what does this mean? 13 But others were mocking and saying, they are full of sweet wine.

What’s happening here? The people heard the apostles speaking in all the languages of those present. See Bonus Material for more on other instances where speaking in tongues is recorded.

They were astonished and didn’t know how to explain what was happening, so they accused the disciples of being drunk and confused. (This is an odd explanation, as drunk people don’t suddenly speak intelligently in other languages!)

Acts 2 is a wonderful chapter for understanding the purpose of speaking in tongues. It begins with the disciples receiving the holy spirit. In verses 5-11, the apostles begin speaking in tongues to a large crowd. The rest of the chapter continues with Peter speaking about the repentance of sins and the fulfillment of prophecy. Toward the end, verse 41, we see that 3,000 were converted and baptized as a result of hearing the message in their own language. From this passage, we see the purpose of speaking in tongues was to preach and spread the gospel message.

14 But Peter, taking his stand with the eleven, raised his voice and declared to them: Men of Judea and all you who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you and give heed to my words. 15 For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is only the third hour of the day (meaning 9 am); 16 but this is what was spoken of through the prophet Joel.

Once again, those who were so perplexed were given an immediate answer: the prophet Joel predicted the holy spirit – God’s power and influence – would be given. Expected prophecy was being fulfilled at this moment, so it shouldn’t be this shocking. Peter went on to explain who Jesus was and the call to follow him.

This type of doubt arises when something completely out of the ordinary occurs. These uneducated Hebrew men are suddenly speaking other languages. The tongues of fire, representing God’s holy spirit, had come upon them just before this. This dramatic event had people asking, What is this? This can’t possibly be real! How can they know how to do this? It is just so far beyond normal. Immediately after the event, Peter explains this is a fulfillment of the prophet Joel’s prophecy (Joel 2:28-32).

After both of these examples, the women at Jesus’ tomb and the Day of Pentecost’s miraculous happenings, there was an immediate revealing of God’s will and His plan. Out of the perplexity, they were brought to a higher appreciation. In these cases, there was serious perplexity in the context of unexpected developments. They were difficult situations. What were they supposed to do with the unexpected? Let’s look at defining this kind of doubt.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: Sometimes things develop that simply leave us at a loss. As we examine whatever comes before us, let us be sure to focus on the scriptural basis of what we see and the capacity to embrace that which is godly. Our perplexity can open the door to God’s ways.

We have to allow that perplexity to open us up to ask, Lord, what does this mean? How do I see this in relation to scripture or to prophecy? How do I see what is happening from your perspective, not mine?

That’s the beauty of being nonplussed. It stops us and makes us think, so it’s often a prime opportunity to be open to a deeper understanding or putting things together for an elevation of faith. We want a perspective where our faith can grow higher, not get stuck rehearsing the doubt again and again. We search to see how God’s will is being performed through these things in a scriptural fashion.

For the women, they ran back to tell the others that Jesus was resurrected. They were able to give a message of hope.

Here at Pentecost, they listened to Peter’s explanation and committed to following Jesus. This sudden stop in their attention allowed them to respond to what was happening as being God’s will and a fulfillment of prophecy.

The last example is regarding the Apostle Peter and his vision that would open the door for Gentiles to be called to Christ. Let’s look at the context of the verse where the perplexity occurs.

Peter doesn’t know this, but Cornelius, a Gentile and a Roman centurion who had been secretly faithful to the God of Israel for years, received a vision of an angel of God (Acts 10:3-4). The angel tells him to send his men to find Peter’s house and to bring Peter back with them.

While Cornelius’ men are on their way, Peter is praying but is hungry. He also sees a vision, but his vision is of a large sheet coming out of the sky, lowered by four corners to the ground. On the sheet were all kinds of animals, reptiles and birds – what the Jewish Law would consider both clean and unclean animals to eat. Peter hears a voice telling him to eat the animals, but he protests, saying he has never eaten anything forbidden by the Law.

Acts 10:9-11: 9 …as they were on their way and approaching the city (Joppa), Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. 10 But he became hungry and was desiring to eat; but while they were making preparations, he fell into a trance; 11 and he saw the sky opened up, and an object like a great sheet coming down, lowered by four corners to the ground.

The voice commands him not to say something is forbidden if God says it is not. This vision repeats three times and this sheet is raised back up to heaven. The message is very straightforward. What God has called clean is clean. No questions, no comments, no But what about? God is making a clear, unequivocal statement. How could Peter understand this after generations and generations of doing something one way under God’s Law, and now being confronted with the opposite?

What God has called clean is clean indeed:

Acts 10:17: Now while Peter was greatly perplexed <1280> in mind as to what the vision which he had seen might be, behold, the men who had been sent by Cornelius, having asked directions for Simon's house, appeared at the gate.

Peter was greatly perplexed – nonplussed – frozen with doubt over what to do next. I’m supposed to eat unclean food? What was unclean is now clean? How am I supposed to apply this? What does it have to do with me? And wait. WHO’S at the door?! There is this flood of information that comes in and he just does not know how to react. Peter was immediately given a clear path to follow in the midst of his perplexity:

Acts 10:19-20, 22: 19 While Peter was reflecting on the vision, the spirit said to him, Behold, three men are looking for you. 20 But get up, go downstairs and accompany them without misgivings <1252> (without wavering, without any doubt), for I have sent them myself. 22 They said, Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous and God-fearing man well-spoken of by the entire nation of the Jews, was divinely directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and hear a message from you.

This is serious perplexity in the context of unexpected future direction because Peter had a limited perception due to his loyalty to the Law. How did his limited perception change? It was God’s spirit within him showing him what to do, how to do it and why to do it. This wasn’t some voice shouting out loud at him, it was God’s spirit moving within him, showing him that this is exactly what God’s plan is dictating. He must follow. It is a very strong direction that was given and Peter obviously does follow.

This was a tremendous, unexpected development. The lesson was given in a shocking, repeating vision, and Peter was told he was now allowed to eat all kinds of foods. But he was immediately given the understanding that this went way beyond food. This prepared him to look at the Gentile nations in a different way. (Source: Matthew Henry Concise Commentary) “The prejudices of Peter against the Gentiles would have prevented his going to Cornelius unless the Lord had prepared him for this service. To tell a Jew that God had directed those animals to be reckoned clean which were hitherto deemed unclean, was in effect saying, that the law of Moses was done away.”

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: Sometimes the direction we are called upon to go may be completely out of context with what we know. At such crossroads let us find peace in the providence of God’s direction for us, as we seek to do His will according to His word and not our own.

We do not make up a story that fits our inclinations. We need to follow God’s word very carefully.

Peter later had to stand firm in arguing for the expansion of the gospel while others had serious doubts. They had the same doubts Peter would have had, but they had not received the vision.

At the conference in Jerusalem Peter recounted the clear direction that he was given to go to Cornelius and his household:

Acts 15:8-10: 8 And God, who knows the heart, testified to them giving them the holy spirit, just as He also did to us; 9 and He made <1252> no distinction <1252> between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. 10 Now therefore why do you put God to the test by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? He made no distinction - God did not hesitate to give the Gentiles His spirit, therefore, why would we hesitate? Peter’s testimony cleared up the misinformation that Jewish Christians were holding on to.

In each of these three “nonplussed” experiences, there was a history-changing event: - The resurrection of Jesus. - The giving of the holy spirit at Pentecost to the Jewish Christians. - The giving of the holy spirit to the Gentiles.

Those who were perplexed were given immediate answers about what was happening.

Some of us will have this kind of stop-you-in-your-tracks kind of doubt at one time or another. We don’t initially know how to react, but we can find the answer. For me, what comes to mind is the tragedy of 9/11. I was frozen with the horror of it and it led me to making the final decision in giving my heart to the Lord. There is plenty of fear out there due to current world events that can cause people to doubt the Lord’s hand in it all, or they will cling to Him even closer. God’s will can be detected even in the big picture of things that do not look easy to understand. It seems odd, but serious doubt and perplexity can actually be an attention getter for us to find the pathway that God wants us to follow.

Doubt can show itself as hesitation, wavering and all out perplexity. How much further and deeper can it go?

Our next level of doubt is very similar to the previous perplexity. The main difference seems to be that in the previous examples there were choices as to how we decided to interpret something. In those cases we could compare and choose what to hold onto. As we shall now see, this next kind of doubt feels more like being trapped. Let’s look at this final Greek word for doubt: Loss: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #639 aporeo; to have no way out, i.e. be at a loss (mentally) King James Version translates this word as doubt 2 times, be perplexed 1 time, stand in doubt 1 time Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to be without resources, to be in straits, to be left wanting, to be embarrassed, to be in doubt, not to know which way to turn

2) to be at a loss with one’s self, be in doubt

3) not to know how to decide or what to do, to be perplexed Perplexity: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #640 aporia; a (state 0f) quandary Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: the state of one who is in perplexity

The verb and noun versions are aporeo and aporia. There is no longer the “di” prefix. Here it is “apo,” meaning away, off, detached, a separation. There is no sense of having a choice. The feeling of having no way out can be ominous. These words are not used often in the New Testament but when they are used, they teach us valuable doubt-altering lessons.

This is another level. This word takes away the “this way or that way” choice in a doubt decision. This puts us in a position nobody wants to be in of feeling like there is no way out.

The first example is the perplexity that 11 of the 12 experienced with Jesus the night before his crucifixion:

John 13:21-22: 21When Jesus had said this, he became troubled in spirit, and testified and said, Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will betray me. 22 The disciples began looking at one another, at a loss <639> to know of which one he was speaking.

At a loss - aporeo - there’s no way out – one of you in this room will betray me. They didn’t know Judas was the one, so we can imagine each one thinking, Is this something I’m capable of? Even accidentally?

The idea of one of them betraying Jesus was incomprehensible and yet those were Jesus’ words! What Jesus says, Jesus means. They are sitting there saying, It couldn’t be me. I wonder if it is you? I wonder… how could it happen… There is no way out of this. There is no easy answer. It is one of the 12. That is it. There is no, well, it could be this or it could be that. NO, this is serious. This is life-threatening and life-changing right here. There is no way out.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: Sometimes the reality of what is happening around us can simply be hard to believe. In every case, let us look to Jesus’ words and example to find comfort and direction when we cannot easily put our outward circumstances in order.

Instead of wallowing in our own self-pity over being stuck in whatever “no way out” experience we find ourselves in, let us instead look to our Lord and fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). We look to Jesus. While we are not going to be able to walk totally the way he did because we are not perfect, we can take steps in that direction. We can accept our “no way out” by realizing that Jesus had no way out, and yet he was glorified. Let us follow him. Next is the example of the perplexity upon humanity that the end times will bring:

Luke 21:25-26: 25 There will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among nations, in perplexity <640> at the roaring of the sea and the waves, 26 men fainting from fear and the expectation of the things which are coming upon the world; for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

Roaring seas and waves in the Bible often symbolically represent restless humanity. This perplexity is like a tsunami coming, and there’s nowhere to run. You’re trapped and it’s going to overtake you.

That is a depressing scenario. And, sometimes we feel like that, especially in light of big world events. Humanity will have a growing sense of there being no way out and this inevitably leads to fear. And fear often leads to anarchy. But the key for handling all this is that God knows. God allows certain things to happen for a certain period of time so that every man, woman and child who ever lived can have an eternal benefit from experiencing these doubt-producing events. It is like going through surgery. Nobody wants to get cut open. Nobody wants to go through the pain of rehabilitation. But after all is done, we can see what a worthwhile experience it has been. That is how we want to look at this kind of “no-way-out” circumstance.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: In light of the world-changing events that will bring God’s kingdom to its glory, we must always appreciate the difficulties of those around us and be willing to live as examples of hope, faith and trust in the power of God’s eternal plan.

We receive a lot of sad emails and blog comments from people whose doubts have paralyzed them from moving forward. Let’s share some comments: - “I question my baptism and wonder if Jesus is living in my heart. If I have doubt, does it mean I am not really a Christian?” - “I doubt my salvation. I have regret…and I don’t like myself. Is this self-hatred a sign that I’m not saved?” - “I was doing sinful things in my life, but I’ve changed. I still feel like God has not forgiven my sins and as a result, I have stopped doing spiritual work.” - “I repent but fall back into the sin of addiction, sometimes within days or hours, or weeks or months. Am I truly repenting and forgiven each time?” - “My sins are so bad there’s no way God could ever forgive me.”

When we read the comments in context, the first thing we notice is that people don’t fully understand scripturally how repentance and forgiveness work and what exactly is meant by salvation. We will provide additional study resources in the Bonus Material. What about sins that are so wretched they are beyond forgiveness?

If we are going back to God through Christ asking for forgiveness and realizing what we have done, that is not a sin that is wretched beyond forgiveness! It is simply a sin that has overtaken us and buried us in the process. We need to understand that the wretchedness and unforgivableness of our sins are FORGIVEABLE if we are truly repentant. What we are saying when we say our sins are beyond forgiveness, is that the way we see our sin is bigger than the way God sees it.

Most people do not understand repentance and forgiveness the way they ought to because repenting means to change direction – going a different way from the sinful direction. It does not mean just staying in the sin and saying, Forgive me.

When someone has an addiction, for instance, it often is a circumstance that comes back to them. Just because it comes back does not mean that they are not forgiven if they are working on it.

I have had the opportunity of walking with individuals through recovery from addiction. Many times, the person needs professional help, absolutely. But they also need to be reassured that if they fall, it does not mean they are done. It just means they need to get up again with more determination and they need to work even harder. They need support and to forgive themselves as they take steps forward. When we say our sins are bigger than God’s ability to forgive, we are being idolatrous. We are elevating the created (our sins) above the Creator. That ought not to be. God is bigger than any of our sins, but we have to decide to repent from them and to change direction in order to be made clean.

It comes down to a mathematical equation: How many times are we to forgive our brother? 70 times 7! Keep on the pathway of forgiveness. God forgives us over and over again. Our part is to get back up and do our best not to fall into our weaknesses, constantly working on overcoming them. When we stumble, we need to ask God again for forgiveness and the strength to overcome our sin.

This is what we, as followers of Christ, can feel when going through difficult times. Here the Apostle Paul tells us how he felt:

2 Corinthians 4:7-10: 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power will be of God and not from ourselves; 8 we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed <639>, but not despairing; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; 10 always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our body.

The Apostle Paul bares his internal turmoil: - He is perplexed but not despairing – feeling he has no way out of the circumstance he is in, but he is not despairing. - He is persecuted and pursued all the time, but not forsaken. - He is struck down – he was stoned, left for dead – but not destroyed. - He was afflicted in every way, but not crushed.

When we put all of this together, we can see that even when the Apostle Paul felt like there was nothing he could do - he was stuck with no way out - despair DID NOT enter. This is the key to this kind of CONSTRUCTIVE DOUBT.

The internal turmoil of our own life experience can leave us feeling alone in our “no way out” perplexity, but the Apostle Paul said he was always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus… In other words, This is my experience to honor God through Christ. I will take it. I will not despair even if there is no way out.

Defining Doubt’s Building Blocks: The Apostle Paul gives GREAT comfort as he shares with us how he constructively coped with his “no way out” kind of doubts. His ending thought was that ALL of the turmoil of his life was his share of dying with Jesus. What a beautiful thought! Paul saw this as a privilege, and we should strive to see our traumas and doubts the way he saw his.

We get to walk with Jesus. What a beautiful example! This is what our perplexity, our “no way out” experience, is. We want our experiences to bring us to where they brought the Apostle Paul.

Philippians 4:4-7 4 Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I will say, rejoice!

Focus and refocus your heart and mind on the fact that God’s providence is sure. This is not even a question! He knows the beginning from the end. His plan is intact, and it always has been. Rejoice in the Lord. We rejoice in Him, not the experience. 5 Let your gentle spirit be known to all men. The Lord is near.

We need to live that focus in a way that others can see the Christlikeness of our character and say, That person is an inspiration to me. I don’t know what drives them, but they seem unshakeable by the things I can’t handle. Make sure that rejoicing is something that shows on the outside as well as on the inside. 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.

Take your doubts to the throne of grace with gratitude and sincerity. Thank You for Your guidance God, I don’t know what to do. I know You know where I am supposed to go. Help me see what You would have me to see and ignore my own interpretation of things. We must make sure we are thankful, not necessarily for the doubt and difficult circumstances, but for the fact that God allows it to be a part of our life, so that our lives will grow like Peter’s. Let us be O ye of little faith, who can grow into something stronger in Christ because we are putting our focus on him. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

This is where we end up.

Exit destructive doubt and enter maturity! Christian maturity comes as a result of putting doubt in its place. This is an important set of lessons.

In these two episodes, we have attempted to give an overview of doubt and acknowledge it is there. We cannot escape from it, but we can decide to put our destructive doubts behind us.

Other doubts can be steppingstones toward being more like Jesus. This is what our lives are about and what doubt can do for us if we approach it with scriptural faith and focus, by God’s grace.

So, how can I doubt my doubts?

From Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …think about it!

Walking on Water, by Joy Suraci It’s dark. The winds and waves are raging; your boat is tossed.

You cling to the sides of your little boat, the wind and the drizzle spray of water on your face.

You see Jesus standing on the waters, stable and calm.

You see his radiant face, and the penetrating gaze of Love as he watches you.

You hear his voice. “Come closer to me.”

His eyes are fixed on you, with the greatest of love and confidence. He knows that no wave or wind in any storm of circumstance can wrest you from his power or his reach.

You heed his voice and leave the boat of your security to come closer. All your attention is fixed on him, and the roar of the storm seems like a dull hum in this moment.

And you realize this is the relationship I have been called to.

And this Holy Relationship provides the resources to approach any challenge. Whether he chooses to calm the literal storm or not, he can calm the storm in my heart.

And he will call me closer to himself. And even if we get distracted by the wind and the waves and begin to sink, he is ready to immediately stretch forth his hand and lift us up.

Matthew 14:22-33 Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives.

Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid.” John 14:27 “My peace,” is a peace demonstrated to us in Christ throughout his ministry and as he faced the most challenging of experiences, even to the death of the Cross. We pray for this peace, a conviction past and beyond all emotion, that KNOWS that he is with us, ready to impart his strength and draw us closer.

Ep. 1303: How Can I Doubt My Doubts? (Part II) See: https://christianquestions.com/character/doubts-part-ii/

1. How did the Pharisees mock Jesus on the cross? In what way did they fulfill the prophecy of Psalm 22? What were the actions of the Pharisees we must never copy and why? (Matthew 27:41-43, Psalms 22:6-8)

2. Mildest kinds of doubt – diakrino and distazo

a. What prefix is used on many of the words for “doubt”?

b. What does this prefix mean?

3. How do 1 Corinthians 6:4-6 and James 1:5-8 illustrate this?

a. What does “double-minded” mean and why must we not be so?

b. How does Abraham’s faith contradict this kind of wavering? How was he rewarded? (Romans 4:19-22)

c. In what way can our own doubts become obstacles or tools? How should we handle our own vacillations? Is this kind of doubt constructive or destructive?

4. Was Jesus rebuking Peter for his doubt while walking on the water? Explain. Why did Jesus’ voice initially frighten the disciples in the boat? Why might Jesus have said, You of little faith, to Peter who exhibited a great faith in stepping out of the boat? How was his doubt constructive? (Matthew 8:25-27, 14:22-33)

5. Do you have a doubt of faith? Use the five suggested questions to find out the source of your doubt and dismantle it so you can turn it from destructive to constructive doubt that will help you to grow.

6. Stronger kinds of doubt – diaporeo

a. What does “nonplussed” mean? At times of dramatic perplexity, what does the Lord provide?

b. What did the women at Jesus’ tomb do with the perplexity of their unmet expectations? (Luke 24:1-10)

c. What was the crowd’s reaction at Pentecost when the apostles spoke in tongues? (Acts 2:12-16)

d. How did God reveal His will and plan after these unexpected happenings?

e. Why was Peter perplexed at the visions he was given? What was his limited perception? How did he react to the revealing of God’s plan for the Gentiles? (Acts 10:17-22, 15:8-10)

7. Strongest kind of doubt – aporeo, aporia

a. What distinguishes aporeo from diaporeo?

b. What was frightening about Jesus’ proclamation on the night before his crucifixion? (John 13:21-22)

c. How can we handle the perplexity we know will come to earth before God’s kingdom? (Luke 21:25-26)

d. How do repentance and forgiveness work?

e. Why is 2 Corinthians 4:7-10 a good role model for us? How does Paul make his perplexity constructive?

8. Describe the beautiful steps laid out for us in Philippians 4:4-7. How can you be like Peter, O ye of little faith, by refocusing your doubt on Jesus?

## Episode 829 — What Happens When Life Gets Broken?
Published: 2014-08-31
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/society/829-what-happens-when-life-gets-broken/

1 Corinthians 10:13: (NASB) No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it.

Tragedy is a part of life. We all know those who have suffered through it. Many times it gets the best of people, and sometimes people cope, but occasionally you find those who truly overcome it, to a point that the tragedy is merely a memory and can serve as a tool of growth and example. Today we will tell such a story. It is a true story of bad things happening and how faith in God, perseverance and the right help transformed those bad things into overcoming lives...

## Episode 879 — The Gay Marriage Law – How Do We Respond?
Published: 2015-08-16
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/society/879-the-gay-marriage-law-how-do-we-respond/

1 Timothy 2:5-6: (KJV) 5For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

Special Guest: David Stein The world is changing. It is changing at an ever-quickening pace and in a more dramatic and fundamental way than ever, as well.

Within the last few months, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of gay marriage, changing the definition of a 6,000 year-old institution. In terms of scriptural study, if you want to understand something we need to look not only at the words but also the context in which they are used. Often the writer will define what he (or she) means by a word, not just by the one

way he uses it in one verse, but also by several ways he uses it in several verses. In Romans 2:14 Paul uses the exact same word, “nature.”

Romans 11:24: (KJV) For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature <5446>, and wert graft contrary to nature <5446> into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural <5446> branches, be graft into their own olive tree?

Heather Barwick mother and her mother’s same-sex partner raised this author. She is a former gay marriage advocate turned children's rights activist.

She is a wife and mother of four rambunctious kids.

Dear Gay Community: Your Kids Are Hurting Gay community, I am your daughter. My mom raised me with her same-sex partner back in the ’80s and ’90s. She and my dad were married for a little while. She knew she was gay before they got married, but things were different back then. That’s how I got here. It was complicated as you can imagine. She left him when I was two or three because she wanted a chance to be happy with someone she really loved: a woman.

My dad wasn’t a great guy, and after she left him he didn’t bother coming around anymore.

Do you remember that book, “Heather Has Two Mommies”? That was my life. My mom, her partner, and I lived in a cozy little house in the ‘burbs of a very liberal and open- minded area. Her partner treated me as if I was her own daughter. Along with my mom’s partner, I also inherited her tight-knit community of gay and lesbian friends. Or maybe they inherited me?

Either way, I still feel like gay people are my people. I’ve learned so much from you. You taught me how to be brave, especially when it is hard. You taught me empathy. You taught me how to listen and how to dance. You taught me not be afraid of things

that are different. And you taught me how to stand up for myself, even if that means I stand alone.

I’m writing to you because I’m letting myself out of the closet: I don’t support gay marriage. But it might not be for the reasons that you think.

Children Need a Mother and Father It’s not because you’re gay. I love you, so much. It’s because of the nature of the same-sex relationship itself.

Growing up, and even into my 20s, I supported and advocated for gay marriage. It’s only with some time and distance from my childhood that I’m able to reflect on my experiences and recognize the long-term consequences that same-sex parenting had on me. And it’s only now, as I watch my children loving and being loved by their father each day, that I can see the beauty and wisdom in traditional marriage and parenting. Same-sex marriage and parenting withholds either a mother or father from a child while telling him or her that it doesn’t matter. That it is all the same. But it’s not. A lot of us, a lot of your kids, are hurting. My father’s absence created a huge hole in me, and I ached every day for a dad. I loved my mom’s partner, but another mom could never have replaced the father I lost.

I grew up surrounded by women who said they didn’t need or want a man. Yet, as a little girl, I so desperately wanted a daddy. It is a strange and confusing thing to walk around with this deep-down unquenchable ache for a father, for a man, in a community that says that men are unnecessary. There were times I felt so angry with my dad for not being there for me, and then times I felt angry with myself for even wanting a father to begin with. There are parts of me that still grieve over that loss today.

I’m not saying that you can’t be good parents. You can. I had one of the best. I’m also not saying that being raised by straight parents means everything will turn out okay. We know there are so many different ways that the family unit can break down and cause kids to suffer: divorce, abandonment, infidelity, abuse, death, etc. But by and large, the best and most successful family structure is one in which kids are being raised by both their mother and father.

Why Can’t Gay People’s Kids Be Honest?

Gay marriage doesn’t just redefine marriage but also parenting. It promotes and normalizes a family structure that necessarily denies us something precious and foundational. It denies us something we need and long for, while at the same time tells us that we don’t need what we naturally crave. That we will be okay. But we’re not. We’re hurting.

If anyone can talk about hard things, it’s us.

Kids of divorced parents are allowed to say, “Hey, mom and dad, I love you, but the divorce crushed me and has been so hard. It shattered my trust and made me feel like it was my fault. It is so hard living in two different houses.” Kids of adoption are allowed to say, “Hey, adoptive parents, I love you. But this is really hard for me. I suffer because my relationship with my first parents was broken. I’m confused and I miss them even though I’ve never met them.”

But children of same-sex parents haven’t been given the same voice. It’s not just me. There are so many of us. Many of us are too scared to speak up and tell you about our hurt and pain, because for whatever reason it feels like you’re not listening, that you

don’t want to hear. If we say we are hurting because same-sex parents raised us, we are either ignored or labeled a hater.

This isn’t about hate at all. I know you understand the pain of a label that doesn’t fit and the pain of a label that is used to malign or silence you. And I know that you really have been hated and that you really have been hurt. I was there, at the marches, when they held up signs that said, “God hates fags,” and “AIDS cures homosexuality.” I cried and turned hot with anger right there in the street with you. But that’s not me. That’s not us.

I know this is a hard conversation. But we need to talk about it. If anyone can talk about hard things, it’s us. You taught me that.

## Episode 1347 — Did a Belief in Hell Always Exist? (Hellfire Series Part IV)
Published: 2024-08-19
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1347-origin-hellfire-series-part-iv/

Did a Belief in Hell Always Exist? (Hellfire Series Part IV)

Genesis 2:16-17: 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die.

The subject of eternal torment can be volatile as there are so many variations in its explanations. Aside from all of the questions and debates regarding the interpretation of Scripture, there’s one fundamental question that often gets overlooked. If a hell of torment is the ultimate consequence for sin, did God’s people always know that? Think about the power of this question. For the many Christians who see the eternal torture of hell as a deterrent from sin, wouldn’t God in His justice have given all of His people through all of history ample knowledge of this overwhelming consequence? Is the doctrine of eternal torment plainly revealed throughout the whole Bible? When do we see this teaching revealed in any ancient pagan belief system?

We’re going to overlay pagan history onto the Old Testament history. It is very revealing! As with each episode in this Hellfire Series, we want to state right up front our understanding of Scripture on this important topic.

Our firm belief is the doctrine of hell as eternal torment did NOT have its beginnings in Scripture, but in several very ancient, pagan civilizations. Over thousands of years we believe that the influence and power of these pagan beliefs corrupted the perspectives of many who claimed to hold to the sacredness of biblical Scripture. The end result left many with unjustified fears of a horrific afterlife never proclaimed by God! Our scriptural proof begins with God’s first command and consequence:

Genesis 2:16-17: 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die (literally translated from Hebrew as “dying thou shalt die”).

If torment was really the penalty, why wasn’t God more specific right from the beginning at the first mention of death as the penalty for sin?

This simple scriptural proclamation was directly contradicted by Satan as he spoke to Eve:

Genesis 3:4-5: 4 The serpent said to the woman, You surely will not die! 5 For God knows that in the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.

It was here that Satan’s “thread of deception” was put into action. Should we believe God or Satan? Well, of course we should believe God!

Watch how this thread of deception (the lie of not dying) blossomed into something that becomes magnetic to belief systems. This lie of not dying has taken hold of mankind. A hell of torment is a direct outgrowth of that lie!

4,000 years after the proclamation of death for sin to Adam, the Apostle Paul repeated the exact penalty that God had proclaimed:

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ.

As far as we can tell, it began with ancient Egypt: (Source: The Hell of Ancient Egypt, by John Watson, touregypt.net) The principal sources for our knowledge of the Egyptian concept of hell are the Books of the Netherworld which are found inscribed on the walls of the royal tombs of the New Kingdom in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes, and then later on papyrus and other funerary objects belonging to commoners.

These writings are dated during the 18th dynasty of Egypt which began when Moses was young. Remember, Egypt became an enemy of God's people. While enslaved, Israel developed into an entire nation while in Egypt.

They would have known Egyptian customs and beliefs. Remember, the Ten Plagues were against the gods of Egypt. Once free, for the first time they were given a written Law clearly establishing their allegiance to God only.

It’s thought that each of the Ten Plagues intentionally targeted a different god of Egypt. For example, the first plague of turning the water to blood was a direct confrontation against the Egyptian god of the Nile, a water bearer named Hapi. The ninth plague of three days of complete darkness was against Ra, the Egyptian god of the sun. God’s supremacy over the Egyptians’ false gods was demonstrated with each plague (see Bonus Material). (Source: The Hell of Ancient Egypt, by John Watson, touregypt.net) The concept of hell in the ancient Egyptian religion is very similar to those of our modern religions. Those who were judged unfavorably faced a very similar fate to our modern concept of hell, and perhaps even more specifically to the more Middle Age concept of it as a specific region beneath the earth. For the damned, the entire, uncontrollable rage of the deity was directed against those who were condemned through their evils. They were tortured in every imaginable way and "destroyed," thus being consigned to nonexistence. They were deprived of their sense organs, were required to walk on their heads and eat their own excrement. There is more which we won’t get into, but this is the afterlife the ancient Egyptians believed in. That was the context within which Israel was enslaved.

With this Egyptian belief system as background, we go to the first text of the Old Testament that some interpret as a reference to hellfire.

The following texts were written between 1400-1500 BC:

Deuteronomy 32:21-22: (KJV) 21 They have moved Me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked Me to anger with their vanities: and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

This is the consequence—to have you replaced, not to burn you forever. Hell: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7585: sheol Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew to English Lexicon: underworld, grave, hell, pit The King James Version translates this word as “grave” 31 times, “hell” 31 times and “pit” 3 times, total 65 times

Sheol has nothing to do with torture or even consciousness. It’s the state of being dead or “sleeping” in the grave.

The Apostle Paul’s quotation of this text from Romans 10:19-21 relates to the casting off of Israel and the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. Sheol is the grave, symbolizing destruction. They perished―the King James Version substitutes pit for Sheol here. SECTION I. DESCRIPTION OF THE HEATHEN HELL.

Among the ancient pagans, the belief in a hell of some sort was very general, if not universal. It was known by various names, as Orcus (named after the god of the underworld), Erebus (meaning darkness), Tartarus, and Infernus or Inferna, whence our expression "infernal regions," etc. The views…respecting it were different at different periods, and among different nations, according to the degree of civilization. The concept was everywhere―except in Jewish culture. Let’s jump forward in time by about 600 years from around 1400-1500 BC to 850 BC. Scripturally, this is around the time of Elijah the prophet.

Hell’s location: It was supposed to be as far below the earth (or as deep down in it), as the heavens are above it. Hesiod, the Greek poet, who lived 850 BC is very precise in his statement, and says, “a mass of iron would be nine days falling from heaven to earth, and nine more in falling from earth to hell.”

Remember, at this time it was widely thought the earth was flat. They are trying to show how far up heaven is above and how far hell is below. The human imagination is limitless! Despite the pagan mythological beliefs, up to the point of Moses, Israel does not have any concept of a burning hell in the Old Testament. We are pushing forward now to Elijah’s time.

While Israel at this time was not generally swayed by Greek culture from the previous quote from Hesiod, they were steeped in the mire of Canaanite culture and fighting idolatry as illustrated by Elijah confronting the priests of Baal. (Source: Gotquestions.org, “Who was Baal?”) According to Canaanite mythology…Baal was considered the most powerful of all gods, eclipsing El (the chief god of the Canaanite pantheon of gods) who was seen as rather weak and ineffective. In various battles Baal defeated Yamm, the god of the sea, and Mot, the god of death and the underworld…The Canaanites worshiped Baal as the sun god and as the storm god—he is usually depicted holding a lightning bolt—who defeated enemies and produced crops. How did God address the Baal issue? Remember how He dealt with the gods of Egypt as we see how God used Elijah to deliver His message: - First, there was no rain for several years—Baal was a storm god, yet they had no rain, showing Baal’s weakness. - Next, rain only came again when Elijah said it would, showing God’s dominant power or influence. - Lastly, God sent fire down to consume Elijah’s sacrifice while Baal, the lightning bolt-bearer, could do nothing!

Baal could do nothing even though these were supposed to be his powers! This is how God operated. He didn’t enter into the pagan ritualistic thinking, nor did He allow His people to “borrow” it from those around them. God showed such practices and thinking to be mythological―made up―because that is what it was.

Now we move ahead in time to the 7th century BCE. At this time in the Bible, the prophet Jeremiah is on the scene. Let’s check in with the pagans of the ancient Persian Empire of the time. The great Persian Empire was in present-day Iran. (Source: A primary historical resource, The Origin and History of the Doctrine of Endless Punishment by Thomas B. Thayer, New and enlarged edition. Boston: Universalist Publishing House. 1881.) THE HEATHEN INVENTED THE DOCTRINE OF ENDLESS PUNISHMENT—SHOWN BY THEIR OWN CONFESSIONS. (Blue is added by CQ.) The national religions of Greece and Rome were the inventions of the legislator and the priest for the purpose of governing and restraining the common people. ...all the early lawgivers claim to have had communications with the gods, who aided them in the preparation of their codes.

Zoroaster, the religious philosopher, claimed to have received his laws from a divine source; Lycurgus, the lawgiver of Sparta in ancient Greece, obtained his from the Greek god Apollo, Minos the king of Crete from the Greek god Jupiter, Numa, the second king of Rome from Egeria, a nature deity in Greek folklore, the Greek lawgiver Zaleucus from Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, etc. The object of this sacred fraud was to impress the minds of the multitude with religious awe, and command a more ready obedience on their part.

The early lawgivers claimed to have gotten their code of law from mythological characters. When fear rules, obedience is the only survival choice. — Toni Morrison These Pagan cultures kept the thread of deception going to justify Satan's original lie—you surely will not die.

Chapter IV. The Jews Borrowed the Doctrine from the Heathen It is allowed on all hands (meaning “it is commonly accepted”) that the Jews in our Saviour's time believed the doctrine of future endless punishment; that it was a part of the common faith. Of course, as the doctrine is nowhere to be found in their Scriptures, the question arises, where did they find it? At the close of the Old Testament Scriptures they did not believe it; at the beginning of the New Testament they did.

Let’s go to the last book of the Old Testament to one verse of Malachi’s prophecy:

Malachi 4:4: Remember the Law of Moses My servant, even the statutes and ordinances which I commanded him in Horeb for all Israel.

The command was to hold onto ALL of what God had given them. The Law, with its statutes and ordinances, was their only foundation. There was going to be a period of silence, and they needed to hold onto what they knew. They weren’t to be corrupted by what looked enticing in the beliefs of those nations surrounding them.

Malachi was the last of the Hebrew prophets, and from him to Christ there stretches this waste period of four centuries…And all this while they were in constant and close intercourse with the heathen, especially the Egyptians, the Greeks and Romans, who held the doctrine in review as part of the national faith. From these, therefore, they must have borrowed it.

The Jews adopted the idolatry surrounding them. It seemed that this teaching came in from outside.

During this time, we can note the great detail with which this hellfire teaching was explained. Polybius (circa 200 – c. 118 BC) was a Greek historian of the Hellenistic Period noted for his work, The Histories, which covered the period of 264–146 BC in detail. Polybius wrote, "Since the multitude is ever fickle, full of lawless desires, irrational passions and violence, there is no other way to keep them in order but by the fear and terror of the invisible world; on which account our ancestors seem to me to have acted judiciously, when they contrived to bring into the popular belief these notions of the gods, and of the infernal regions." In other words, Polybius is saying: This is a good thing because there’s no way to keep these fickle crowds in order, other than with the threat of eternal misery. We can have a peaceful society even though every human being is living in fear.

Belief compelled through fear is not belief; it is blind and forced obedience. — Carlton D. Pearson Fear creates obedience. It’s that simple.

A FUTURE day of judgment, using a furnace of fire (not the underworld) as a SYMBOL of judgment. Once again, God delivers judgment within a time frame and NOT for eternity! We went over this in detail in Part II of this Hellfire Series, Episode 1342: What Does “Weeping and Gnashing of Teeth” mean?

Publius Vergilius Maro (October 15, 70 BC – September 21, 19 BC), usually called Virgil or Vergil in English, was an ancient Roman poet of the Augustan period. Virgil lived about 50 years before Jesus was on the earth, towards the end of that 400 years between the end of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New.

This is what he said about punishment in the afterlife in his epic Latin poem called the Aeneid: And now wild shouts and wailing dire and shrieking infants swell the dreadful choir. Here sits in bloody robes the Fury* fell, by night and day to watch the gates of hell. Here you begin terrific groans to hear, and sounding lashes rise upon the ear. On every side the damned their fetters grate, and curse, 'mid clanking chains, their wretched fate. *Fury: a spirit of punishment, often represented as one of three goddesses who executed the curses pronounced upon criminals, tortured the guilty with stings of conscience, and inflicted famines and pestilences. The Furies were identified at an early date with the Eumenides (Greek deities of vengeance).

All the while, God has given Israel a Law where they are punished in this life in a just way, not coming remotely close to any of these dreadful torments of these other belief systems in their afterlife. This next example is JUST before John the Baptist and Jesus will appear on the scene.

Strabo was a Greek geographer, philosopher and historian who lived between 64 or 63 BC to 24 AD.

Strabo wrote, "...For it is impossible to govern the crowd of women, and all the common rabble, by philosophical reasoning, and lead them to piety, holiness and virtue—but this must be done by superstition, or the fear of the gods, by means of fables and wonders; for the thunder, the aegis*, the trident, the torches (of the Furies), the dragons. etc., are all fables, as is also all the ancient theology. These things the legislators used as scarecrows to terrify the childish multitude." *aegis: shield or breastplate of protection through supernatural power; associated with Zeus and Athena. **Furies: a spirit of punishment, often represented as one of three goddesses who executed the curses pronounced upon criminals, tortured the guilty with stings of conscience, and inflicted famines and pestilences. The Furies were identified at an early date with the Eumenides (Greek deities of vengeance).

So, in the ancient world of Greece just before Jesus lived on this earth, the “legislators” not only adopted this thought of an afterlife of torture and torment, but the ones in power knew this was made up. They deliberately used the fear of the unknown as a tool to keep people in line.

It is a simple tool, easy to use, so why not? Just make up horrible fiction and perpetuate the myth.

The process is easily understood. About three hundred and thirty years before Christ, Alexander the Great had subjected to his rule the whole of Western Asia, including Judea, and also the kingdom of Egypt. Soon after he founded Alexandria, which speedily became a great commercial metropolis, and drew into itself a large multitude of Jews, who were always eager to improve the opportunities of traffic and trade. A few years later, Ptolemy Soter (a Macedonian Greek general, historian and successor of Alexander the Great) took Jerusalem, and carried off one hundred thousand of them into Egypt. Here, of course, they were in daily contact with Egyptians and Greeks, and gradually began to adopt their philosophical and religious opinions, or to modify their own in harmony with them.

The word “conflation” comes to mind―the merging of two or more sets of information, texts, ideas, or opinions into one—often in error. This all gets jumbled together.
